title: Categorical perception does not mean listeners hear nothing inside a category
trap: Categorical perception means listeners cannot detect any difference between sounds in the same category.
text: Categorical perception means within-category differences are much harder to hear than equal differences across a boundary. In Liberman and colleagues (1957), within-category discrimination was near chance but real accuracy was a little above what labels predicted. McMurray and colleagues (2003) found that sounds closer to the boundary drew more looks to the competitor word. So listeners keep graded information about how good an example a sound is, even when their final label is the same.

title: A step-like identification curve does not prove thresholded processing
trap: If listeners’ labels switch sharply, phoneme processing must be thresholded.
text: A sharp labeling curve only describes the final answer. In McMurray and colleagues’ study, clicks were step-like, but eye movements to the competitor rose gradually near the boundary. A thresholded model sends the same finished phoneme for every /b/, so it cannot produce that gradual change. So the labels can be categorical while the processing behind them is cascaded.

title: The Ganong effect is a boundary shift, not a general bias
trap: The Ganong effect just means listeners prefer to report real words everywhere on the continuum.
text: A general reporting bias would make the lexical effect the same size at every step. Ganong found the effect small at the endpoints and largest near the boundary. Only ambiguous sounds leave room for word knowledge to decide the phoneme. So word knowledge shifts the boundary itself, which TRACE explains with feedback from words to phonemes.

title: Broca’s comprehension deficit may not be a loss of grammar
trap: Caramazza and Zurif proved that Broca’s aphasia destroys grammatical knowledge.
text: Caramazza and Zurif (1976) found that Broca’s patients fail when syntax conflicts with common sense, and that was taken as evidence for a syntax deficit. Dick and colleagues then found that healthy undergraduates under stress show the same trouble with object clefts and passives. Saygin and colleagues (2004) also found Broca’s patients impaired on nonverbal action matching. So the deficit may be a performance issue, or broader than language, rather than lost grammar.

title: Broca’s own patients were not Broca’s aphasics in the modern sense
trap: Broca’s original patient Tan is the classic example of agrammatic Broca’s aphasia.
text: Tan could produce only one syllable but seemed to understand what was said. Broca’s actual patients were arguably unable to produce speech at all, apparently because of motor control problems. Today they would be classified as having apraxia of speech. So the modern description of Broca’s aphasia as a grammar problem is fairly distant from Broca’s cases.

title: Infants do not start out able to hear every contrast
trap: Infants are citizens of the world who can hear all speech contrasts and only lose them.
text: That narrative fits Werker and Tees (1984), where non-native contrasts fade by 10 to 12 months. But Narayan and colleagues (2010) found that four-month-olds cannot readily hear /na/ versus /ŋa/, whatever their language. Filipino-learning infants only detected it by 10 to 12 months, after exposure. So development also builds some contrasts, and not all contrasts are available innately.

title: Adults are not worse learners in every way
trap: Children learn a second language faster than adults.
text: Adults actually learn faster at first, because of transfer from L1 and better general cognitive skills. A child knows only about 20 words after 18 months of exposure. Adults do worse in ultimate attainment, since they rarely become native-like. So speed and final success are separate, and the sensitive period concerns final success.

title: In the Revised Hierarchical Model, the strong lexical link runs from L2 to L1
trap: Because L1 is stronger, activation must spread more easily from L1 words to L2 words.
text: The L1 lexicon is larger and more strongly linked to concepts. But the strong lexical link runs forward from L2 words to L1 words, because that direction is emphasized in learning. Strong L1 conceptual links explain why a partly active Russian word, spichki, could activate the concept of matches and draw the eyes. In the Russian task, English words have weak conceptual links, so they cause no reliable interference.
